analysis.one_liner: Bans nursing homes from forcing residents to sign away their day in court.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee 17-10 and was reported to the full House on September 26, 2008, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing homes and assisted-living facilities routinely put an arbitration clause in the stack of admission paperwork, so if a resident is neglected or injured, the family's only option is a private arbitrator chosen under the facility's contract — not a judge or jury. This bill would make such pre-dispute arbitration clauses invalid and unenforceable for long-term care residents, leaving them free to take disputes to court. It passed committee but never got a House floor vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home and assisted-living residents and their families, who would keep the right to sue in court over abuse, neglect, wrongful death, or billing disputes instead of being routed into private arbitration signed away at admission — often by a family member under pressure during an emergency move-in.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Makes any pre-dispute arbitration agreement between a long-term care facility and a resident (or a person acting for the resident, including one with financial responsibility) invalid and not specifically enforceable [S2] [S3].

Covers a broad range of long-term care settings, including skilled nursing facilities, nursing facilities, and assisted-living-type facilities providing help with bathing, dressing, eating, and medication [S3].
Applies to agreements signed during or after the admission process, so facilities cannot get around the ban by obtaining the clause later [S3].
Puts the decision on whether an agreement is enforceable in the hands of a court rather than an arbitrator, and makes federal law govern that question [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Long-term care providers, who would face jury trials and larger damage awards over abuse, neglect, and wrongful death claims instead of private arbitration, plus the arbitration industry, which would lose this stream of cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Long-term care providers and arbitration firms

drawbacks.text: Critics of arbitration bans argue that court litigation is slow and expensive, and that arbitration can resolve resident disputes faster and at lower cost than a jury trial; honest supporters must acknowledge that some families would get resolution more slowly in court [S3].

The bill does not ban arbitration outright — a resident could still agree to arbitrate after a dispute arises — but it leaves nursing homes fully exposed to lawsuits from the date of enactment for new agreements, which the industry contended would raise liability costs passed on in care prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted at one of the most vulnerable populations: people who sign admission packets while arranging care for a dying or incapacitated relative rarely read the arbitration clause, and pre-dispute clauses effectively strip them of a public trial over abuse or neglect. The cost is higher litigation exposure for facilities and, plausibly, some of that cost passed to care prices; the strongest counterargument — that arbitration is cheaper and faster — applies poorly to cases where the signer lacked genuine consent and the disputes involve serious injury or death. A narrow, well-designed consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved and reported the bill in September 2008 and it was placed on the House calendar, but the House adjourned at the end of the 110th Congress without ever taking it up, so the bill died.

narrative.text: Introduced May 22, 2008 by Rep. Linda Sánchez with a small bipartisan group including Republican Ileana Ros-Lehtinen, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S5].
Referred June 6 to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, which held a hearing on June 10, marked the bill up on July 15, and forwarded it to the full committee on a 5-4 vote [S5].
The full Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported on a 17-10 vote on July 30, and it was formally reported with House Report 110-894 on September 26, 2008 [S5].
Placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 577), the list of bills awaiting House floor consideration, but no floor vote ever occurred before the 110th Congress ended January 3, 2009 [S5].
The bill gathered 23 cosponsors, 22 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Long-term care facilities keep the ability to require residents to sign away their right to sue, and arbitration providers keep the business; residents and families gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators and arbitration firms

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 22 Democrats to 1 Republican — and while the bill cleared committee 17-10, the House as a whole never voted, so full-chamber partisan lines never materialized.

industries.note: Nursing homes and assisted-living operators use pre-dispute arbitration clauses in admission paperwork to channel resident injury and death claims away from juries into private arbitration. The bill would end that practice, exposing them to court litigation — the direct cost of giving residents their day in court.

Private arbitration firms and the attorneys who administer facility contracts would lose a stream of disputes involving some of the most vulnerable consumers. Their business depends on the clauses the bill voids.

Personal injury firms representing nursing home residents would gain access to jury trials, which typically produce larger awards than arbitration. Their gain runs alongside residents' restored right to sue.
